chapter_theme: Twenty verses of about five things each, opening with a matched pair on the precocious and the dull, then moving through renunciation in youth, a bad wife, teacher and pupil, penance defined by conduct, a ladder of giving, penance and knowledge, beauty as speech, and the soldier who spares the surrendered.

21.reading: There are trees that fruit without flowering, and those who know the good and are skilled in books are elders without having aged; there are seeds that sprout without being sown, and to the intelligent understanding reaches without being told.
21.nuance: Two nature images each answered by a kind of person: the tree that fruits unflowered is the young man who is already an elder in knowledge, the seed that sprouts unsown is the quick mind that needs no telling. Divided into five, taking நன்றறிவார் and நூல்வல்லார் as two descriptions; they could be one. Verse 22 is its exact negative.

items.claim: there are trees that bear fruit without first flowering
those who know the good are elders without having aged
those skilled in books are likewise elders without age
there are seeds that sprout without being sown
to the intelligent, understanding goes home without being spoken

22.reading: There are trees that flower yet do not fruit, and men who, though grown old, do not grasp the books; there are seeds that do not sprout even when buried in a bed, and to the fool understanding does not reach even when told.
22.nuance: The mirror of verse 21, image for image: flowering without fruit is age without learning, the buried seed is the fool who is told and still does not take it. Line 2 as printed (மூவாது மூவர்நூல் தேற்றதார்) does not construe cleanly; the reading takes it as the aged who have not understood the books, as the parallel with 21 requires. Four things, not five.

items.claim: there are trees that flower and still do not fruit
there are men who do not grasp the books though they have aged
there are seeds that do not sprout even when buried in a prepared bed
to the fool, understanding does not reach even when spoken

23.reading: Those who rely on five things (bodily form, youth, the beauty that has come to them, a family that bows to no one, and lineage) and do not renounce while young never see the unshaken state that has no end.
23.nuance: Two of the five are pride of birth (குடி, குலம்), set beside the body's goods as things that hold a man back. The deadline is youth itself (இளங்கால்): renunciation put off past youth is the failure. Line 3's தொக்(கு)ஈர் பசுவால் is obscure; it may speak of being dragged by bound attachment, and the reading leaves it out.

items.claim: bodily form is one of the five things relied on by those who do not renounce young
youth is one of them
the beauty one happens to have is one of them
a family that bows to none is one of them
lineage is one of them

24.reading: The verse names as the doings of a bad wife drinking toddy, living apart from her husband, going without shame into other people's houses, prying with intent into others' affairs, and keeping close ties with bad women.

norm.note: a rule of the period for a wife's conduct, listing what marks a bad wife

24.nuance: All five faults lie outside the kitchen and the husband's presence: drink, absence, other houses, other people's business, bad company. காணில் in line 1 is hard to place (if one looks, or when he is seen). Line 3-4's கிளைமைத் துறமது is doubtful; it may instead mean cutting off her own kin, and the fifth item is held loosely.

items.claim: drinking toddy is a bad wife's doing
living apart from her husband is a bad wife's doing
going shamelessly into others' houses is a bad wife's doing
prying with intent into others' affairs is a bad wife's doing
close ties with bad women are a bad wife's doing

25.reading: The verse urges joining those of great character, not seizing another's wealth, giving up the friendship of the dark-natured and guarding against evil speech, for Death's coming is certain and the reckoning is not mere talk.
25.nuance: Four commands and then their ground: the coming of காலன் is certain, and the last line (வழக்கு is not mere mouth-talk) says the judgment that follows is real. The list's force comes from the fifth item, which is not a command at all but the reason for the other four.

items.claim: those of great character are to be joined
another's wealth is not to be seized
the friendship of the dark-natured is to be left
evil speech is to be guarded against
Death's coming is certain, and the reckoning is not mere words

26.reading: The sky-bird's nest, lac, the white silkworm's work, the fit of a stick and honey are things no one can make at will; the skilled should not say they achieve whatever they set out to, for to each single being some one thing comes without fail.
26.nuance: The five are works of creatures (the weaver bird's nest, the lac insect, the silkworm, perhaps the termite or bee, the honeybee) that no human craftsman can copy, set against the boast of the skilled. கோல்தகுதல் is obscure and the fourth item is a guess. The point is a limit on human skill: every being has its own one gift.

items.claim: the nest of the sky-bird cannot be made by anyone at will
lac cannot be made by anyone at will
the white silkworm's work cannot be made by anyone at will
the fitting of a stick (sense obscure) cannot be done by anyone at will
honey cannot be made by anyone at will

27.reading: The man set in dharma stands on the good path, the unrestrained outsider does not leave the low path, and the one who befriends outsiders picks up toddy, theft and gambling and, practised in them, shows them as of old.
27.nuance: The verse turns on நாட்டான்/நட்டான், the one established and the one who befriends: vices are learned through company. The construal of lines 2-4 is uncertain; the division takes two persons and three vices.

items.claim: the man established in dharma stands on the good path
the unrestrained outsider keeps to the low path
toddy is what the friend of outsiders picks up and displays
theft is what he picks up and displays
gambling is what he picks up and displays

28.reading: The teacher is one who seeks no gain from men, the pupil who suits him serves him with love, the pupil who learns everything has cast off the three, and for one who has not cast them off all that he holds remains a disease of the heart.
28.nuance: Divided into four: teacher, loving pupil, the pupil who has cast off the three, and the one who has not. The three are not named; in a Jain work they are most likely desire, anger and delusion, the three the invocation says the Lord destroyed (மூன்றொழித்து). Learning without that riddance is called a sickness, not a lesser good. ஆண்ஆக்கம் may mean worldly gain or a man's advancement; the reading takes gain.

items.claim: the teacher is one who seeks no gain
the pupil fit for him serves him with love
the pupil who learns all has cast off the three
for one who has not cast them off, all he holds is a disease of the heart

29.reading: The verse sets out a student's observances: hair kept as a tuft like a closing neytal bud with the rest trimmed, a term of a month, and the student's work of reciting the text and listening, coming to the teacher with a bow and circling him to the right.

norm.note: a rule of the period for a student's tonsure and his ritual approach to the teacher

29.nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to construe: உய்தல் ஒருதிங்கள் நாளாகும் may give the interval for trimming the hair or a period of study. துணங்கு in line 3 is obscure. The second half is clearer: recitation, listening, bowing and circumambulation of the teacher.

items.claim: the student's hair is a tuft like a neytal bud
reciting the text is the student's work
listening is the student's work
the students come bowing
the students circle the teacher to the right

30.reading: There is no one who knows everything, no one who knows nothing at all, no one wholly without fault with every virtue held in him, and no one who has learned the whole body of the treatises.
30.nuance: Four negations, each closed by the single இல் at the end. The second is the surprise: as no one is all-knowing, no one is wholly ignorant either, so the verse limits contempt as much as pride.

items.claim: there is no one who knows everything
there is no one who knows nothing at all
there is no one wholly faultless with all virtues in him
there is no one who has learned the whole body of treatises

31.reading: If a man does no harm to living beings, forgets the pain that befalls him, does no hurtful wrong to another, and gives up desire and anger, the diseases that are faults, then penance is not lowly but sweet.
31.nuance: Penance is defined wholly by conduct, with no rite or austerity named. மறத்தல் (forgetting) the pain that comes goes further than enduring it. The conclusion answers a doubt the verse assumes: that penance is a lowering of oneself.

items.claim: not harming living beings makes penance sweet
forgetting the pain that befalls one makes penance sweet
not doing hurtful wrong to another makes penance sweet
giving up desire makes penance sweet
giving up anger makes penance sweet

32.reading: The verse says that he who performs sacrifice is the brahmin, chastity is the excellence of a bright-jewelled woman, he who listens is the flawless great scholar, a poet's excellence comes from his mind, and in the world one's good comes through the father.

norm.note: the period's definition of the brahmin by the sacrifice and of a woman's excellence by chastity

32.nuance: Each line names a person by the act that makes him what he is called. பார்ப்பான் is a birth term, but the verse ties it to the act of sacrifice (வேட்பவன்), not to birth; it reports that norm, it does not argue it. The last item gives the father, not one's own deeds, as the source of standing in the world.

items.claim: he who performs the sacrifice is the brahmin
chastity is the excellence of a woman
he who listens is the flawless great scholar
a poet's excellence comes from his mind
in the world one's good comes through the father

33.reading: The verse says that only he who lays up is the liberal man and he who hands out is a merchant, that only he who leads to the higher state is a teacher, and that the one so led, keeping the body's hedge and never beginning to eat flesh, is sure to go there.
33.nuance: The first line is a paradox whose sense is uncertain: the 'laying up' is perhaps the store of merit made by giving, and the 'handing out' giving for return, so that the merchant gives and the liberal man saves. The closing rule makes abstaining from flesh the test of whether one has been led upward.

items.claim: only he who lays up is the liberal man
he who hands out is a merchant
only he who leads to the higher state is a teacher
the one led keeps the body's hedge closed
if he never begins to eat flesh, his going is certain

34.reading: Blame comes of reviling, homage comes of doing good, a thriving family comes of what was done before, enjoyment comes of wealth, and dharma comes of grace that has melted.
34.nuance: Five effects, each with its cause. The division of lines 1-3 (வசை / வணக்கம் / செழுங்குலம்) is uncertain; செழுங்குலம் may instead be the fruit of homage. The last two repeat verse 2's pairing of wealth with enjoyment and grace with dharma, and add that the grace must be நெகிழ்ந்த, softened.

items.claim: blame comes from reviling others
homage comes from doing good
a thriving family comes from deeds done before
enjoyment comes from wealth
dharma comes from grace that has melted

35.reading: Surveying the good dharma of householders and the dharma of renunciation, the verse says that giving brings enjoyment, penance brings heaven, and knowledge brings release.
35.domain_note: surveys both the householder's and the renouncer's dharma
35.nuance: Three ranked paths with three ranked fruits, and heaven is only the middle one: release belongs to knowledge, not to penance. Only three things, not five. போதும் in line 3 is read as போகம், enjoyment; as printed it does not construe.

items.claim: giving brings enjoyment
penance brings heaven
knowledge brings release

36.reading: The beauty of the hair, of the eye-catching chest, of the nails, of the ears and of faultless teeth is not beauty; the beauty of speech fitted to learning is beauty.
36.nuance: Five bodily beauties are denied and a sixth affirmed, so the verse counts six; the last undoes the first five. The true beauty is not learning as such but speech that fits the books (நூற்கியைந்த சொல்).

items.claim: the beauty of the hair is not beauty
the beauty of an eye-catching chest is not beauty
the beauty of the nails is not beauty
the beauty of the ears is not beauty
the beauty of faultless teeth is not beauty
the beauty of speech fitted to learning is the true beauty

37.reading: The verse says, addressing a young woman, that the worthy do not eat food got by bowing, do not sleep in a friend's house, do not seize another's property that has gone astray, do not look down on one after joining with him, and do not take up baseness after a quarrel.
37.nuance: The subject is unstated, and taken as the worthy. புலை in line 4 is read as baseness of conduct, not as the caste term. தொழீஇ அட may also mean food cooked by one made to bow, that is, by a servant forced to it.

items.claim: the worthy do not eat food got by bowing
the worthy do not sleep in a friend's house
the worthy do not seize another's property that has gone astray
the worthy do not look down on one after joining with him
the worthy do not take up baseness after a quarrel

38.reading: Not lying is good, wealth is good, not killing so that a life suffers is good, not exalting oneself before many is, when weighed, worth esteem, and the minds of the excellent shun unworthiness however small.
38.nuance: Wealth stands between the two vows as a plain good, with no ranking among the three. Lines 3-4 are hard to divide; the reading takes பேணாமை as not making much of oneself and மாணாமை as unworthiness that the excellent mind will not admit.

items.claim: not lying is good
wealth is good
not killing so that a life suffers is good
not exalting oneself before many is worth esteem
even small unworthiness is shunned by the minds of the excellent

39.reading: To put a treasury, many accounts, oversight, a kitchen of food and a household in the charge of men without understanding to match their size is like setting a crow to guard cooked rice.
39.domain_note: the master who appoints officers to his stores and accounts
39.nuance: The five are offices of trust in a great house; பாத்தில்லார் உண்டார் and தோழரில் are hard to construe and the last two items are held loosely. The measure of the appointee is understanding fit to his body: a big man with a small mind.

items.claim: a treasury given to the witless is like rice guarded by a crow
the many accounts given to them are the same
oversight given to them is the same
the kitchen's food given to them is the same
the household given to them is the same

40.reading: Those who have dropped their clothing, those who chew grass, those who have entered running water, those who have laid down their weapons and those who have fled with nothing left: these five, the verse says, true soldiers never go near.
40.nuance: All five are signs of a beaten or helpless enemy: stripped, grass in the mouth in surrender, taking to the river, weapon down, in flight. The restraint is made the mark of the true (செவ்வகை) soldier, not a mercy he may choose.

items.claim: those who have dropped their clothing are never approached by true soldiers
those who chew grass are never approached
those who have entered running water are never approached
those who have laid down their weapons are never approached
those who have fled with nothing are never approached

links.note: Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength on seeing they do not last; Sirupanchamoolam 23 says those who rely on form, youth, beauty, family and lineage and do not renounce young never see the unshaken state.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives impermanence as the reason to renounce; the verse adds a deadline, youth itself, and a second obstacle, pride of birth, so delay and lineage join transience as what keeps a man from release.
links.list_adds: It sets family and lineage (குடி, குலம்) in the same list as the body's goods and makes youth both an item and the time limit.

links.note: Naladiyar 363 names three bad wives (the defiant, the one who skips the kitchen, the one who withholds food) as weapons that kill the husband; Sirupanchamoolam 24 names five doings of a bad wife.
links.teaches: The quatrain's faults all lie inside the house and against the husband, the verse's all lie outside it (drink, absence, other houses, prying, bad company), so together they show the period's norm for a wife policing both her service and her movements.
links.list_adds: Its five faults face outward from the house, where the quatrain's three are failures of service within it.

links.note: Purananuru 195 tells aged worthies that the axe-bearing one will bind them, so if they cannot do good they should at least avoid harm; Sirupanchamoolam 25 sets four commands under the certainty of Death's coming.
links.teaches: Both rest counsel on the certainty of death, but the Sangam poem bargains down to a minimum (at least do no harm) while the ethics verse turns the same ground into four positive and negative rules and adds a reckoning after death.

links.note: Verse 20 lists not stealing, not gambling and not befriending the black-hearted among five abstentions; verse 27 says the friend of outsiders picks up toddy, theft and gambling.
links.teaches: Verse 20 puts bad company beside theft and gambling as one more abstention; verse 27 shows it as their cause, so the book's ban on bad friends is a ban on the way the other vices are learned.

links.note: Purananuru 183 says learning is good even at the cost of serving the teacher, giving him wealth and accepting the lower place; Sirupanchamoolam 28 says the true teacher seeks no gain and the fit pupil serves with love.
links.teaches: The Sangam king accepts payment and service as the price of learning; the Jain verse keeps the pupil's loving service but denies the teacher any gain, and adds that learning without casting off the three faults is a sickness.

links.note: Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and life is short, so the wise choose what to learn; Sirupanchamoolam 30 says no one has learned the whole of the treatises, and no one knows all or nothing.
links.teaches: The quatrain draws from the boundlessness of learning a method of choosing; the verse draws from the same limit a judgment of persons: no one is complete in knowledge or virtue, and no one wholly lacks knowledge either.
links.list_adds: It sets the limit of learning beside matching limits on knowing, not knowing and faultlessness, so the shoreless field becomes one case of a rule that no person is complete either way.

links.note: Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Sirupanchamoolam 31 keeps both, adds three more, and says penance so made is sweet, not lowly.
links.teaches: The couplet defines penance by two ethical acts; the verse keeps them, turns bearing pain into forgetting it, and meets an objection the couplet does not raise, that penance degrades the one who does it.
links.list_adds: It extends the couplet's two marks to five, adding no wrong to another and the giving up of desire and anger, and closes with a verdict on how the penance feels.

links.note: Kural 134 says a brahmin who forgets the Veda can relearn it but one whose conduct fails loses his birth; Sirupanchamoolam 32 says the brahmin is the one who sacrifices.
links.teaches: Both tie the birth term பார்ப்பான் to something done rather than to birth alone, but the Kural ties it to conduct and the verse to the rite of sacrifice, two different tests for the same status.
links.list_adds: It puts the brahmin's defining act in a row with a woman's chastity, a scholar's listening, a poet's mind and the father's gift, so each kind of person is named by one mark.

links.note: Kural 418 says ears not pierced by listening are deaf though they hear; Sirupanchamoolam 32 says the one who listens is the flawless great scholar.
links.teaches: The couplet condemns the unlistening ear; the verse makes listening the very definition of the great scholar, ranking it above reading or composing.
links.list_adds: It sets the listener beside the poet, whose excellence is in his mind, so hearing and composing are named as two separate excellences.

links.note: Kural 255 says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh and hell will not release the one who eats; Sirupanchamoolam 33 says the one led upward who never begins on flesh is sure to go there.
links.teaches: The couplet threatens the meat-eater with a hell that does not open; the verse promises the abstainer a sure passage, and ties the abstention to the teacher who leads him, so diet becomes the proof of being led.
links.list_adds: It ends a list of true titles (liberal man, merchant, teacher) with abstaining from flesh as the condition of the pupil's passage.

links.note: Kural 247 says that world is not for those without grace as this world is not for those without wealth; Sirupanchamoolam 34 says enjoyment comes of wealth and dharma of melted grace.
links.teaches: The couplet weighs grace against wealth by the worlds they open; the verse gives each its fruit (enjoyment, dharma) and calls the grace melted, so grace is a softening of the heart, not a possession.
links.list_adds: It sets the wealth and grace pair at the end of a chain of five causes and effects, so enjoyment and dharma are results like blame and homage.

links.note: Verse 2 says enjoyment belongs to the man with wealth and dharma to the man with grace; verse 34 repeats the pairing as cause and effect.
links.teaches: The book states the wealth and grace pairing twice; in verse 34 it becomes causal and the grace is qualified as melted, so the second statement tightens the first.

links.note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; Sirupanchamoolam 35 assigns enjoyment to giving, heaven to penance and release to knowledge.
links.teaches: The couplet frees giving from any reward; the verse keeps a reward but ranks it lowest, so both deny that giving is the way to heaven, one by indifference to reward and one by a ladder of rewards.
links.list_adds: It ranks giving, penance and knowledge on one ladder of fruits, enjoyment, heaven, release, which the couplet never builds.

links.note: Verse 5 says one who wants to be rid of the body does penance and one who wants standing gives; verse 35 says penance brings heaven and only knowledge brings release.
links.teaches: Read together, the two verses disagree on what ends embodiment: verse 5 credits penance, verse 35 reserves release for knowledge and gives penance only heaven.

links.note: Naladiyar 131 says beauty of hair, garment and saffron is not beauty and the beauty of learning is; Sirupanchamoolam 36 says beauty of hair, chest, nails, ears and teeth is not beauty and speech fitted to learning is.
links.teaches: Both deny outward beauty to praise learning, but the quatrain rests learning's beauty on fairness of heart, while the verse rests it on speech that fits the books, so one makes it inward and the other audible.
links.list_adds: Its list is all of the body (hair, chest, nails, ears, teeth), not adornments, and it turns on speech rather than learning itself.

links.note: Kural 1033 says all who do not live by their own ploughing bow to eat and walk behind; Sirupanchamoolam 37 says the worthy do not eat food got by bowing.
links.teaches: The couplet names the farmer as the one man free of bowing for food; the verse makes refusing such food a rule of the worthy whatever their trade, so the Kural's economic point becomes a point of self-respect.
links.list_adds: It sets the refusal beside not sleeping in a friend's house and not taking lost goods, so eating by bowing is ranked with small breaches of dignity and honesty.

links.note: Kural 323 ranks not killing first and not lying after it; Sirupanchamoolam 38 calls not lying, wealth and not killing each good without ranking them.
links.teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse declines the Kural's ranking of the two vows and admits wealth among the goods between them, a Jain list that values non-killing without making it the single highest good here.
links.list_adds: It lists not lying, wealth and not killing side by side with wealth in the middle, where the couplet orders the two vows and leaves wealth out.

links.note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Sirupanchamoolam 39 says giving treasury, accounts and stores to men without understanding is setting a crow to guard rice.
links.teaches: The couplet locates the fault in the master's fondness; the verse measures the appointee (understanding that does not match his size) and shows the result as the guard eating what he guards.
links.list_adds: It names the particular offices of trust and closes with the crow image, where the couplet speaks only of trust in general.

links.note: Kural 773 says fierceness is great valour but help to a foe in trouble is its cutting edge; Sirupanchamoolam 40 names five helpless enemies whom true soldiers never approach.
links.teaches: The couplet makes mercy to the fallen the edge of valour as a principle; the verse turns it into signs a soldier can read on the field, and makes the restraint the definition of a true soldier.
links.list_adds: It turns the couplet's one principle into five recognisable signs of surrender or helplessness.

links.note: Purananuru 9 praises a Pandya who warns cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he shoots; Sirupanchamoolam 40 names five who give up in battle and must not be approached.
links.teaches: The Sangam king protects those who never fight by warning them before battle; the verse protects those who stop fighting during it, so together they give both ends of the period's code of sparing in war.

source_issues: 22 line 2: மூவாது மூவர்நூல் தேற்றதார் does not construe; the parallel with 21 suggests a reading such as 'though aged, do not grasp the books'.
24 lines 3-4: கிளைமைத் துறமது is doubtfully divided.
25 line 1: பிறன்பொருள்வெள வன்மின் appears to have வௌவன்மின் split, with ௌ written as ெ + ள.
29 lines 1-3: the first half and துணங்கு are hard to construe.
35 line 3: போதும் is likely a misprint for போகம் (enjoyment), which the triad of fruits requires.
37 line 2: show flags a repaired ௌ and a reading that differs from the site.
39 lines 1-2: பாத்தில்லார் உண்டார் அடிசிலே and தோழரில் are hard to construe.
